Every Pope in order from St. Peter to Leo XIV: number in the line of succession, years as Pope, birth and death, and what each is remembered for.

1 Pope c. 30s – 64 or 67Martyred in Rome, 64 or 67 A Galilean fisherman called by Jesus, who named him the rock on which he would build his Church. Leader of the Apostles, he preached in Jerusalem, Antioch and Rome…
2 Pope c. 67–c. 76Died c. 76 Named by early writers as Peter's first successor in Rome. He may be the Linus greeted by St. Paul in 2 Timothy 4:21.
3 Pope c. 76–c. 88Died c. 88 Also called Cletus. One of the earliest bishops of Rome, remembered in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Tradition holds that he died a martyr.
4 Pope c. 88–c. 97Died c. 97 Author of the Letter of Clement to the Corinthians, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, urging peace and order in that church.
5 Pope c. 97–c. 105Died c. 105 An early bishop of Rome during the reign of Emperor Trajan. Little is known for certain about his life; tradition counts him a martyr.
6 Pope c. 105–c. 115Died c. 115 Led the Roman church in the early 2nd century. Later tradition credits him with introducing the use of blessed water mixed with salt.
7 Pope c. 115–c. 125Died c. 125 An early 2nd-century bishop of Rome, remembered among the martyrs. He is often identified with the Sixtus named in early lists of Roman bishops.
8 Pope c. 125–c. 136Died c. 136 The first bishop of Rome after Peter whose martyrdom is attested by St. Irenaeus. Tradition links him to the custom of Christmas night Masses.
9 Pope c. 136–c. 140Died c. 140 Led the Roman church as Gnostic teachers such as Valentinus and Cerdo arrived in Rome, challenging Christian teaching.
10 Pope c. 140–c. 155Died c. 155 Brother of Hermas, author of The Shepherd. During his time the heretic Marcion was expelled from the Roman church.
11 Pope c. 155–c. 166Died c. 166 Welcomed St. Polycarp of Smyrna to Rome. The two disagreed over the date of Easter but parted in peace and charity.
12 Pope c. 166–c. 175Died c. 175 Known for the generosity of the Roman church, which sent aid to Christians in need, praised in a letter by Dionysius of Corinth.
13 Pope c. 175–c. 189Died c. 189 Led the Church as the Montanist movement spread. St. Irenaeus wrote of him in his list of Roman bishops.
14 Pope c. 189–c. 199Died 199 The first bishop of Rome from North Africa. He pressed churches to celebrate Easter on Sunday, which became the universal practice.
15 Pope c. 199–217Died 217 Guided the Church through debates about the Trinity, assisted by his deacon Callixtus, who managed the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way.
16 Pope c. 218–c. 222Died 222 A former slave who rose to lead the Church. He taught that sinners who repent may be readmitted to communion, and he died a martyr.
17 Pope c. 222–230Died 230 Led the Church during a relatively peaceful period under Emperor Alexander Severus.
18 Pope 230–235Died 235 Exiled to the mines of Sardinia under Emperor Maximinus Thrax, he resigned so the Church could choose a new leader, the first recorded papal resignation.
19 Pope 235–236Died 236 Reigned only about six weeks. Tradition says he collected the records of the martyrs. He was the first pope buried in the Papal Crypt of the Catacomb of St. Callixtus.
20 Pope 236–250Died 250 A layman chosen, according to Eusebius, when a dove settled on his head. He organized Rome into districts for the care of the poor and was martyred under Decius.
21 Pope 251–253Died 253 Elected after persecution, he welcomed back Christians who had lapsed and repented, opposing the rigorist Novatian. He died in exile.
22 Pope 253–254Died 254 Briefly exiled at the start of his reign, he continued Cornelius's merciful policy toward the lapsed. St. Cyprian praised him.
23 Pope 254–257Died 257 Taught that baptism by heretics is valid if done in the name of the Trinity, so converts need not be rebaptized, a view later confirmed by the Church.
24 Pope 257–258Died 258 Beheaded with his deacons while celebrating the liturgy in the catacombs during the persecution of Valerian. St. Lawrence was martyred days later.
25 Pope 259–268Died 268 Rebuilt the Roman church after the persecution of Valerian and organized parishes. He sent aid to Christians in Cappadocia captured by invaders.
26 Pope 269–274Died 274 Wrote on the doctrine of the Trinity and the Incarnation. His reign fell under Emperor Aurelian.
27 Pope 275–283Died 283 Led the Church in a time of relative peace. Little else is known for certain.
28 Pope 283–296Died 296 Reigned in the years before the Great Persecution under Diocletian. Tradition says he was related to the emperor.
29 Pope 296–304Died c. 304 Pope at the start of Diocletian's Great Persecution, the most severe the Church endured.
30 Pope c. 308–309Died 309 Elected after a long vacancy, he reorganized the Roman church after the persecution but was exiled over disputes about readmitting the lapsed.
31 Pope 309Died c. 310 Reigned only a few months before being exiled to Sicily by Emperor Maxentius amid unrest over the treatment of the lapsed.
32 Pope 311–314Died 314 The first pope of the age of toleration. After the Edict of Milan (313) the empire returned church property, and he received the Lateran palace.
33 Pope 314–c. 336Died c. 336 Led the Church during the reign of Constantine, when the Council of Nicaea (325) defined the divinity of Christ and the first great Roman basilicas were built.
34 Pope 336Died 336 Reigned less than a year. He is credited with founding the Basilica of San Marco in Rome.
35 Pope 337–352Died 352 Defended St. Athanasius against the Arians and affirmed the faith of Nicaea at the Council of Sardica.
36 Pope 352–366Died 366 Exiled by the Arian Emperor Constantius II for refusing to condemn Athanasius. Tradition links him to the founding of St. Mary Major.
37 Pope 366–384Died 384 Commissioned St. Jerome to revise the Latin Bible, which became the Vulgate. He honored the martyrs by restoring the catacombs with inscriptions.
38 Pope 384–399Died 399 Issued the earliest surviving papal decretal, giving binding answers on Church discipline to the bishops of Spain.
39 Pope 399–401Died 401 Condemned certain teachings of Origen. St. Jerome praised him as a man of holy life.
40 Pope c. 402–417Died 417 Pope when Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. He firmly asserted Rome's authority and condemned Pelagianism.
41 Pope 417–418Died 418 A Greek who at first hesitated over the Pelagian question, then condemned Pelagianism in his letter called the Tractoria.
42 Pope 418–422Died 422 His election was contested by the antipope Eulalius. He defended the authority of Rome over the churches of Illyricum.
43 Pope 422–432Died 432 Sent bishops to the Council of Ephesus (431), which proclaimed Mary the Mother of God. He sent Palladius to the Christians of Ireland.
44 Pope 432–440Died 440 Rebuilt the Basilica of St. Mary Major to honor Mary as Mother of God after Ephesus, and worked to reconcile the churches of Antioch and Alexandria.

45 Pope 440–461Died 461 His Tome shaped the Council of Chalcedon's teaching that Christ is one person in two natures. He met Attila the Hun and persuaded him to turn back from Rome. A Doctor of the Church.
46 Pope 461–468Died 468 As papal legate he had escaped the "Robber Council" of Ephesus. As pope he strengthened Church order in Gaul and Spain and built churches in Rome.
47 Pope 468–483Died 483 Reigned when the last Western Roman emperor was deposed in 476. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against the Monophysites.
48 Pope 483–492Died 492 Excommunicated the Patriarch of Constantinople over the Henotikon, beginning the Acacian Schism between Rome and the East. An ancestor of St. Gregory the Great.
49 Pope 492–496Died 496 Born in Roman Africa, he wrote that the world is governed by two powers, the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power of kings. Known for his charity to the poor.
50 Pope 496–498Died 498 Sought to heal the Acacian Schism with Constantinople through conciliation.
51 Pope 498–514Died 514 Overcame a long challenge from the rival claimant Laurentius. He supported the Catholics of Africa persecuted by the Arian Vandals.
52 Pope 514–523Died 523 Ended the Acacian Schism in 519 with the Formula of Hormisdas, signed by the Eastern bishops. His son later became Pope St. Silverius.
53 Pope 523–526Died 526 Sent to Constantinople by the Arian king Theodoric. On his return he was imprisoned at Ravenna, where he died, and he is honored as a martyr.
54 Pope 526–530Died 530 Appointed under the influence of King Theodoric. He built the Church of Sts. Cosmas and Damian in the Roman Forum.
55 Pope 530–532Died 532 The first pope of Germanic descent. He confirmed the Council of Orange's teaching on grace against Semi-Pelagianism.
56 Born Mercurius Pope 533–535Died 535 The first pope known to have taken a new name on election, since his birth name honored the pagan god Mercury.
57 Pope 535–536Died 536 Traveled to Constantinople, where he deposed the Monophysite patriarch Anthimus and consecrated a successor. He died there.
58 Pope 536–537Died 537 Son of Pope Hormisdas. He was deposed through the intrigues of Empress Theodora and died in exile. He is honored as a martyr.
59 Pope 537–555Died 555 Held for years in Constantinople by Emperor Justinian during the dispute over the Three Chapters, around the Second Council of Constantinople (553).
60 Pope c. 556–561Died 561 Rebuilt the Church's finances and relief of the poor in an Italy devastated by the Gothic Wars.
61 Born Catelinus Pope 561–574Died 574 Led the Church as the Lombards invaded Italy. He completed the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome.
62 Pope 575–579Died 579 Reigned during the Lombard invasions, as famine and plague struck Rome.
63 Pope 579–590Died 590 Sought help from Constantinople against the Lombards. He died of the plague that swept Rome.

64 Pope 590–604Lived c. 540–604 A monk who reluctantly became pope. He sent St. Augustine to convert the English, cared for Rome's poor, reformed the liturgy and wrote the Pastoral Rule. A Doctor of the Church.
65 Pope 604–606Died 606 Successor of Gregory the Great. He sold the Church's grain during a famine, which made him unpopular.
66 Pope 607Died 607 Obtained from Emperor Phocas recognition of the Roman church as head of all the churches.
67 Pope 608–615Died 615 Converted the Pantheon in Rome into a church dedicated to Mary and all the martyrs, a step toward the feast of All Saints.
68 Pope 615–618Died 618 Also called Deusdedit. A Roman priest of long service, he cared for the clergy and the sick during an earthquake and epidemic.
69 Pope 619–625Died 625 Supported the mission to England and corresponded with King Edwin of Northumbria.
70 Pope 625–638Died 638 Promoted missions in England. He was later condemned by the Third Council of Constantinople for his ambiguous letters on Monothelitism.
71 Pope 640Died 640 His confirmation was delayed more than a year because he refused to accept the Monothelite Ecthesis. He reigned only two months.
72 Pope 640–642Died 642 A Dalmatian who condemned Monothelitism and ransomed captives taken in his homeland.
73 Pope 642–649Died 649 A Greek from Jerusalem who opposed Monothelitism and excommunicated the Monothelite patriarch Pyrrhus.
74 Pope 649–655Died 655 Condemned Monothelitism at the Lateran Synod of 649. Arrested by order of Emperor Constans II, he died in exile in Crimea, the last pope honored as a martyr.
75 Pope c. 656–657Died 657 Elected while Martin I was in exile. He stood firm against pressure to accept Monothelitism.
76 Pope 657–672Died 672 Sent Theodore of Tarsus as Archbishop of Canterbury, who organized the church in England.
77 Pope 672–676Died 676 A Roman monk known for kindness to pilgrims. He restored churches in Rome.
78 Pope 676–678Died 678 Restored Roman churches and reconciled the church of Ravenna to Rome.
79 Pope 678–681Died 681 A Sicilian whose letter guided the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681), which condemned Monothelitism.
80 Pope 682–683Died 683 Confirmed the Third Council of Constantinople. He was noted as a preacher and musician.
81 Pope 684–685Died 685 Obtained the emperor's agreement that a pope could be consecrated without waiting for imperial approval.
82 Pope 685–686Died 686 The first of a series of Eastern popes of this era, born in Syria. He was known for his generosity.
83 Pope 686–687Died 687 An elderly compromise candidate, son of a soldier from Thrace. He reigned less than a year.
84 Pope 687–701Died 701 Introduced the Agnus Dei into the Mass, refused to accept the decrees of the Council in Trullo, and baptized King Caedwalla of Wessex.
85 Pope 701–705Died 705 A Greek who ransomed captives taken by the Lombards and protected Rome.
86 Pope 705–707Died 707 A Greek who decorated Roman churches with fine mosaics and frescoes.
87 Pope 708Died 708 Suffered severely from gout and reigned only about three weeks.
88 Pope 708–715Died 715 The last pope to visit Constantinople before Paul VI in 1967, where he was received with honor by Emperor Justinian II.
89 Pope 715–731Died 731 Commissioned St. Boniface as missionary to the Germans and opposed Emperor Leo III's iconoclasm.
90 Pope 731–741Died 741 Born in Syria, the last pope to seek the Byzantine emperor's approval. He condemned iconoclasm and supported St. Boniface's missions.
91 Pope 741–752Died 752 The last Greek pope of the period. He approved Pepin's anointing as King of the Franks and negotiated peace with the Lombards.
92 Pope 752–757Died 757 Crossed the Alps to seek Frankish help against the Lombards. Pepin's donation of land laid the foundation of the Papal States.
93 Pope 757–767Died 767 Brother of Stephen II. He strengthened the alliance with Pepin and moved relics from the catacombs into Rome's churches.
94 Pope 768–772Died 772 Held the Lateran Council of 769, which set rules for papal elections and condemned iconoclasm.
95 Pope 772–795Died 795 Allied with Charlemagne, who defeated the Lombards. His legates took part in the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which restored the veneration of icons.
96 Pope 796–816Died 816 Crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800, founding the Holy Roman Empire.
97 Pope 816–817Died 817 Traveled to Reims to crown Louis the Pious as emperor.
98 Pope 817–824Died 824 Built and decorated churches in Rome, including Santa Prassede, and gave refuge to Greek monks fleeing iconoclasm.
99 Pope 824–827Died 827 Accepted the Constitutio Romana, defining the emperor's role in Rome. He promoted education for clergy.
100 Pope 827Died 827 A Roman deacon praised for his piety. He died after a reign of about a month.
101 Pope 827–844Died 844 Tried to mediate in the civil wars of Louis the Pious and his sons. He fortified Ostia against Saracen raids.
102 Pope c. 844–847Died 847 Reigned when Saracen raiders sacked St. Peter's Basilica outside the walls of Rome in 846.
103 Pope 847–855Died 855 Built the Leonine Wall around St. Peter's and the Vatican after the Saracen raid, and led the defense of Rome at the Battle of Ostia.
104 Pope 855–858Died 858 His election was briefly challenged by the antipope Anastasius. He worked to help churches in England and the East.
105 Pope 858–867Died 867 A strong pope who upheld the indissolubility of marriage against King Lothair II and asserted papal authority in the dispute over Patriarch Photius.
106 Pope 867–872Died 872 Approved the Slavonic liturgy of Sts. Cyril and Methodius. His legates attended the Fourth Council of Constantinople.
107 Pope 872–882Died 882 Defended Rome against Saracen raids and supported St. Methodius. He was the first pope to be assassinated.
108 Pope 882–884Died 884 Had served as papal legate to Constantinople. He was the first pope known to have been bishop of another diocese before his election.
109 Pope 884–885Died c. 885 Reigned about a year amid factional violence in Rome. He died on his way to an imperial diet.
110 Pope 885–891Died 891 Fed Rome during famine and drought. He forbade the Slavonic liturgy after Methodius's death.
111 Pope 891–896Died 896 A former missionary to Bulgaria. After his death his body was exhumed and put on trial by Stephen VI in the infamous "Cadaver Synod."
112 Pope 896Died 896 Reigned only about two weeks amid the turmoil after Formosus's death.
113 Pope 896–897Died 897 Held the Cadaver Synod against Formosus's corpse. Public outrage led to his imprisonment and death.
114 Pope 897Died 897 Reigned about four months during the turbulent years after the Cadaver Synod.
115 Pope 897Died 897 In a reign of about twenty days, he reburied Formosus with honor and restored those he had ordained.
116 Pope 898–900Died 900 Confirmed the rehabilitation of Formosus and annulled the Cadaver Synod.
117 Pope 900–903Died 903 Crowned Louis III of Provence as emperor. He was praised for his charity.
118 Pope 903–904Died c. 905 Overthrown after about a month and imprisoned. He likely died in prison.
119 Pope 904–911Died 911 Reigned at the start of the period when Rome's aristocratic families dominated the papacy. He rebuilt the Lateran Basilica after an earthquake.
120 Pope 911–913Died c. 913 Reigned about two years while the powerful Theophylact family controlled Rome.
121 Pope 913–c. 914Died 914 Reigned about seven months. His name has never been used by another pope.
122 Pope 914–928Died c. 929 Organized the Christian alliance that defeated the Saracens at the Garigliano (915). He was deposed and died in prison.
123 Pope 928Died 928 Reigned about seven months while Marozia controlled Rome.
124 Pope 929–931Died 931 Reigned about two years under the influence of Marozia. He granted privileges to monasteries.
125 Pope 931–935Died c. 936 Son of Marozia, elected young. He granted privileges to the reforming Abbey of Cluny.
126 Pope 936–939Died 939 Supported monastic reform and invited St. Odo of Cluny to Rome.
127 Pope 939–942Died 942 Reigned under the domination of Alberic II, ruler of Rome.
128 Pope 942–946Died 946 Concentrated on the reform of clergy and monasteries.
129 Pope 946–955Died 955 Supported monastic reform and the expansion of the Church in Germany and Scandinavia.
130 Pope 955–964Lived c. 937–964 Became pope as a teenager. He crowned Otto I emperor in 962, but his worldly life led Otto to have him deposed.
131 Pope 963–965Died 965 A layman installed by Emperor Otto I in 963, after a synod declared John XII deposed. His status was disputed, but he is counted in the official list.
132 Pope 964Died 965 Elected by the Romans after John XII's death while Leo VIII was still claiming the office, he was deposed by Otto I and died in exile in Hamburg.
133 Pope 965–972Died 972 Crowned Otto II co-emperor and established new dioceses, including Magdeburg as a center for missions to the Slavs.
134 Pope 973–974Died 974 Murdered in prison by order of the Crescentii family.
135 Pope 974–983Died 983 Restored order in Rome, opposed simony and supported monastic reform.
136 Born Pietro Canepanova Pope 983–984Died 984 Chancellor of Emperor Otto II. After Otto died, he was imprisoned and died in the Castel Sant'Angelo.
137 Pope 985–996Died 996 Carried out the first recorded formal canonization, of St. Ulrich of Augsburg, in 993.
138 Born Bruno of Carinthia Pope 996–999Lived c. 972–999 The first German pope, a cousin of Emperor Otto III, elected in his mid-twenties.

139 Born Gerbert of Aurillac Pope 999–1003Died 1003 The first French pope and the greatest scholar of his age, who promoted mathematics and astronomy. He established the church in Poland and Hungary, sending a crown to…
